sections.summary: The paper opens by asking where the mind stops and the rest of the world begins. It distinguishes two standard replies -- internalism about skin and skull, and meaning externalism -- then proposes a third: active externalism based on the active role of the environment in driving cognitive processes.
sections.title: Introduction: The Boundary Question

sections.summary: Three problem-solving cases -- mental rotation, button-assisted rotation, and neural-implant rotation -- are used to argue that there is no principled cognitive difference between internal and external processing. Tetris research on physical rotation illustrates epistemic action: action that alters the world to aid recognition and search. The parity principle says that if part of the world functions as a cognitive process were it done in the head, then it is part of the cognitive process.
sections.title: Extended Cognition and Epistemic Action

sections.summary: The coupled system formed by organism and external entity is treated as a cognitive system in its own right. The paper contrasts active externalism with the passive externalism of Putnam and Burge: passive external features are distal and historical, while active external features are in the here-and-now loop and can change behaviour when altered.
sections.title: Active Externalism and Coupled Systems

source_span.end_text: extendedcognitionis a corecognitive process, not anadd-onextra.

sections.summary: The authors address objections: not every cognitive process is conscious; the Naked Mind portability intuition fails because reliable external coupling can be part of the basic package; evolution and development may exploit environmental scaffolding; and language is a central means by which cognition is extended into the world.
sections.title: Portability, Reliable Coupling, and Language

sections.summary: The argument moves from cognition to mind. Inga's ordinary memory and Otto's notebook are presented as functionally analogous: Otto's notebook plays the role of biological memory, so Otto can be said to believe the museum is on 53rd Street before consulting it. Twin Otto shows that belief can differ because of an external notebook, so belief is not simply in the head.
sections.title: From Cognition to Mind: Otto and Inga

sections.summary: The paper defends extended belief against alleged differences in reliability, access, perception, and phenomenology. These differences are argued to be shallow; they do not undermine the functional parity between Otto's notebook and Inga's memory. The discussion also addresses occurrent versus dispositional belief and the role of conscious availability.
sections.title: Defending Extended Belief Against Shallow Differences

sections.summary: The authors explore how far extension should go. They list features that make Otto's notebook clearly count as belief: constancy in life, direct availability without difficulty, automatic endorsement, and past conscious endorsement. More exotic cases such as Filofax, Internet files, and social collaborators may be indeterminate or fail on multiple counts.
sections.title: Criteria and Limits of Extended Belief

source_span.end_text: may be ableto see ourselvesmoretrulyas creaturesof the world.

sections.summary: The final section extends the argument socially and personally. Mental states may be partly constituted by other thinkers when trust, reliance, and accessibility are high; language is a tool that spreads cognitive burden into the world. The extended mind implies an extended self and has moral and social consequences.
sections.title: Social Extension, Language, and the Extended Self
